conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; swing pivots are strength-K fractals unless stated; standard Brooks setups referenced only by name (wedge, double top/bottom bear flag, final flag, two-bar reversal) are primitives from earlier chapters and are not redefined here

candidates.name: StairsPatternDetection
candidates.quote: A stairs day is a variant of a trending trading range day where there are at least three trading ranges...The day has broad swings, but trending highs and lows.
candidates.description: Primitive: at least N consecutive swing legs with trending highs and lows (each swing low above the one before it and each swing high above the one before it, for a bull stairs; mirrored for bear), where each breakout also retraces back past its own breakout point before the next leg (overlap between consecutive swings).
candidates.pseudocode: count = 0; for k in 1..maxLegs-1: (swingLow[k] > swingLow[k+1]) && (swingHigh[k] > swingHigh[k+1]) && breakoutOverlap(k); if all true, count++; stairsDetected = count >= (minStairs - 1)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, a run test across several pivots, and an overlap test between consecutive legs

notes: Related to T22-10 (higher swings inside a range) but adds the overlap requirement and treats the whole thing as a with-trend channel, not a range about to break out.

candidates.name: BreakoutOverlapIsNormalInStairs
candidates.quote: Almost every breakout is followed by a pullback (a breakout test) beyond the breakout point, so that there is some overlap between consecutive swings.
candidates.description: Filter: once a stairs pattern is detected, a pullback that retraces past the most recent breakout point (but stays short of the prior opposite swing extreme) is expected and normal -- it should not by itself be read as a trend failure, and countertrend entries into it are reasonable two-sided trades rather than reversal bets.

complexity.reason: a level comparison against the stairs state from T26-01

candidates.name: MinorSwingOvershootDoesNotFlipTrend
candidates.quote: There is sometimes a swing or two that will extend above the prior swing high by a little. This will make some traders wonder if the market is reversing, but the trend will usually soon resume.
candidates.description: Filter: within an established stairs pattern (bear variant), a swing high extends a little beyond the most recent prior swing high (within a tolerance), but this alone does not flip the trend classification; require the overshoot to exceed a larger tolerance, or persist for more than one leg, before treating it as an actual reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: stairsDetected && swingHigh[0] > swingHigh[1] && (swingHigh[0] - swingHigh[1]) <= overshootToleranceAtr * atr -> stairsDetected remains true

complexity.reason: reads swing-pivot state from T26-01 plus a tolerance-banded overshoot test

candidates.name: ShrinkingStairsMomentumWaning
candidates.quote: If each breakout gets a little smaller than the prior one, then this is a shrinking stairs pattern and a sign of waning momentum, which can lead to a larger correction.
candidates.description: Filter: within a stairs pattern, each successive breakout leg's extension (swing extreme minus the prior swing extreme) is smaller than the one before it for at least K legs; this shrinking-stairs signature warns of waning momentum and an increased chance of a deeper (often two-legged) correction or a trend-line-break reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: stairsDetected && for k in 0..shrinkLegs-2: legExtension[k] < legExtension[k+1]; all true -> shrinkingStairs = true

complexity.reason: reads swing-pivot state plus a monotonic-decrease test over consecutive leg sizes

candidates.name: FadeBreakoutUsingPriorExtensionSize
candidates.quote: Traders pay attention to how many ticks breakouts run past the most recent swing point, and then use that number to fade subsequent breakouts, expecting a breakout test. For example, if the last swing low fell 14 ticks below the swing low before it, traders will look to scale into longs beginning around 10 ticks below the most recent swing low.
candidates.description: Entry (mirrored, buy side shown for a bear stairs): in a detected stairs pattern, scale into longs once price trades a fraction of the prior leg's extension size below the most recent swing low, anticipating the usual breakout-test pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order below the most recent swing low, scaled by the typical extension size

complexity.reason: reads the remembered stairs leg-extension history and projects a fraction of it as an offset

notes: Only for experienced traders per the book; beginners are told to use stop entries instead (see T26-07).

candidates.name: ExitAtTypicalRetracementDistance
candidates.quote: If the pullback from the most recent breakout was about 15 ticks, they will look to take profits around 10 to 15 ticks up from the low, which will usually be around the trend line.
candidates.description: Exit: for the fade entry in T26-05, take profit once price rallies a fraction of the typical (most recent) pullback size above the entry/swing low.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order near the trend line

complexity.reason: arithmetic on a remembered pullback-size measurement

candidates.name: ScalpFadeStrongBreakoutInEstablishedStairs
candidates.quote: Once the market begins to form stairs down, you can usually fade the close of every strong trend bar breakout for a scalp. Buy every bear trend bar that closes below a prior bear stair for a scalp.
candidates.description: Entry (mirrored, long side shown): in an established bear stairs pattern, a strong bear trend bar closes below the low of the most recent stair (swing low); buy at the next open (or at the close, per the book) for a scalp back toward the range.
candidates.pseudocode: stairsDetected && bearTrendBar[0] && close[0] < swingLow[1]  /* buy signal, next open; mirrored: sell a bull trend bar closing above the prior stair's high */
candidates.book_order_type: market order at the close of the breakout bar (book's stated method); the book itself prefers a stop entry as price reverses, which is the mechanized close-and-next-open form

complexity.reason: a bar-classification test against the remembered swing-low state from T26-01

notes: The book explicitly says 'it is safer to enter on a stop as the market reverses' rather than at the close -- the close-based pseudocode already matches this project's stop-entry convention (signal-bar-close then next-open).

candidates.name: StairAccelerationChannelMeasuredMove
candidates.quote: The breakout should extend to about a measured move up to a parallel line that is about the same distance from the middle line as the middle line is from the bottom line (an Andrew's Pitchfork move).
candidates.description: Exit/target: when one stair accelerates and breaks out of the channel in the with-trend direction, project a target using the channel's own width -- a line parallel to (and as far from) the channel's middle line as the middle line is from its far boundary.
candidates.pseudocode: channelWidth = middleLine.at(0) - farBoundaryLine.at(0); target = middleLine.at(0) + channelWidth; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the projected parallel line

complexity.reason: needs the trend-channel's three reference lines (trend line, channel line, and their midline) projected from swing pivots

candidates.name: WedgeTopFailureAccelerationMeasuredMove
candidates.quote: The acceleration upward is typical when a wedge top fails. The failed wedge was followed by about a measured move up equal to about the height of the wedge.
candidates.description: Exit/target: when an apparent wedge-top reversal pattern instead fails and price accelerates through it in the prior trend's direction, project a target at the failure point plus the wedge's own height (top minus bottom).
candidates.pseudocode: wedgeTopFailed && target = wedgeBreakoutPoint + (wedgeTopPrice - wedgeBottomPrice); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the measured-move target

complexity.reason: wedge (three-push) detection plus a measured-move projection; the bullish mirror of T24-10's failed-wedge-down case

chapter_summary: Chapter 26 covers stairs days: a broad, sloping channel of at least three trending swings where every breakout is retested (overlap between consecutive legs is normal), shrinking leg sizes warn of waning momentum, and one stair can suddenly accelerate into a stronger trend or a failed wedge. Minable content is dominated by structural, swing-pivot-heavy primitives (stairs detection, overlap normality, minor-overshoot tolerance, shrinking-stairs momentum test) and the trading tactics they license (extension-sized countertrend fades with matching retracement targets, simple close-based scalp fades against the most recent stair, and two measured-move exit projections for acceleration/failed-wedge breakouts). No genuinely non-mechanical statements were found to reject in this short chapter; named setups (wedge, double top, final flag, two-bar reversal) are referenced only by name and were not redefined.
